content: Professionals must act decisively when they suspect maltreatment, ensuring their response prioritizes the best interests of the child. They must also recognize the critical importance of preventing young children from experiencing the detrimental effects of family separation. Strategies to reduce child and domestic violence should include initiatives such as fathers’ support groups, national awareness campaigns, parenting programs, and the involvement of local community champions. Solutions should aim to preserve family unity wherever possible. Concrete commitments and collective action are essential to implement strategic measures and achieve the vision outlined in the Nurturing Care Framework. Governments and relevant stakeholders have pledged their support to the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health, forming a foundation for further commitments to promote nurturing care. This framework calls for individuals and organizations at all levels to collaborate towards achieving relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) targets and proposed milestones at both national and global levels. Global stakeholders have established effective mechanisms for multi-sectoral coordination and harmonized actions to support nurturing care. All countries are incorporating nurturing care into their national communication strategies and leveraging community structures and local leaders to promote it. Global stakeholders have launched a global advocacy campaign to promote nurturing care and effective community engagement approaches, empowering communities to take action. A harmonized global indicator and measurement framework for nurturing care is now available and being utilized to assess implementation and impact. Governments, parliamentarians, and policymakers are expected to commit to a vision of equity and human development, with young children and their families at the center. They should coordinate policies, budgets, operational plans, workforce development, training, tools, and activities across various sectors to support nurturing care. Resources—human, technical, and financial—must be allocated to strengthen policies, information, and services at all levels. A whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach is necessary to support nurturing care. Civil society should advocate for increased attention and investment in nurturing care, strengthen community capacity to support it, enhance families’ and local stakeholders’ knowledge of young children’s rights, and monitor progress while holding all stakeholders accountable for their commitments. Academic and research institutions should generate new evidence on the benefits and impacts of nurturing care, as well as effective implementation strategies, costs, and cost-effectiveness. They should also adapt proven interventions and programs to serve specific groups, including indigenous and hard-to-reach communities, integrate nurturing care into professional training, and disseminate information on evidence and innovations widely. The business community should invest in creating an enabling environment for nurturing care in workplaces, communities, and society by allocating resources and implementing corporate policies that provide adequate and equal paid maternity and paternity leave. The media should advocate for the most deprived populations, raise awareness, promote best practices in nurturing care, and help shift social norms about early childhood using current scientific knowledge. The United Nations and other multilateral organizations should consolidate evidence into a coherent approach, develop norms and guidance, provide technical and financial assistance to countries and partners, monitor progress in policy and intervention coverage, quality, and outcomes, and work in partnership to keep nurturing care high on the sustainable development agenda. Bilateral development partners and philanthropic institutions should mobilize financial and technical resources, stimulate research and innovation, and support the implementation and monitoring of national policies and plans for nurturing care. The Nurturing Care Framework provides a roadmap for action, supported by online resources to facilitate adaptation in different countries. The website will evolve in collaboration with stakeholders, offering information on countries’ progress and resources to guide policymaking and programming. These resources will include policy guidance, advocacy and communication tools, service capacity-strengthening tools, monitoring and evaluation guidance, country stories, and recent research findings. Caregivers are individuals closely attached to a child and responsible for their daily care and support. This includes parents, families, and others directly responsible for the child at home, as well as caregivers in organized daycare settings. Developmental delay refers to a young child’s delayed progress in one or more areas compared to peers, including gross and fine motor skills, speech and language, cognitive and intellectual abilities, social and emotional skills, and executive functions. Developmental difficulty encompasses any condition that risks suboptimal development or causes developmental deviations, delays, disorders, or disabilities. This includes children facing hunger, social deprivation, low birth weight, cerebral palsy, autism, sensory problems, cognitive impairments like Down syndrome, or physical disabilities such as spina bifida. Disability involves challenges in three interconnected areas: impairments in body functions or structures, limitations in executing activities, and restrictions in life participation. Disability arises from the interaction of health conditions with environmental and personal factors. Early childhood development spans children’s cognitive, physical, language, motor, social, and emotional growth from conception to age 8, with the Nurturing Care Framework focusing on the period from pregnancy to age 3. Epigenesis refers to DNA modifications that do not alter the DNA sequence but influence gene activity, determining whether genes are turned on or off. Epigenetic changes occur naturally and can be affected by factors such as age, environment, lifestyle, and disease. A family-centered approach tailors policies, procedures, and practices to address children’s and families’ needs, beliefs, and cultural values. This approach involves partnering with families, recognizing, and building on their strengths. Nurturing care is an environment created by caregivers that ensures children’s health and nutrition, protects them from threats, and provides opportunities for early learning through emotionally supportive and responsive interactions. A whole-of-government approach involves public-service agencies working across portfolio boundaries to achieve shared goals, producing an integrated government response to specific issues. This approach aims to achieve policy coherence to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of policies and programs. A whole-of-society approach involves all relevant stakeholders—individuals, families, communities, intergovernmental organizations, religious institutions, civil society, academia, media, voluntary associations, and, when appropriate, the private sector and industry—working together to support national efforts. This approach strengthens coordination among stakeholders to enhance the effectiveness of their efforts.
